opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that we've been optimizing for the wrong thing, or at least for an incomplete thing.

For the past several years, what I'd call the "first half" of AI, the main game was about methods and models. Someone proposes a new architecture or training method, like the Transformer, RLHF, or reasoning with reinforcement learning, and then shows it beats the previous state of the art on some benchmark. The benchmark was almost an afterthought. We'd take an exam, a math competition, or a game, and climb it. That loop worked incredibly well. Now we have a fairly general recipe: large-scale pretraining, plus reasoning, plus RL. That recipe can basically crush any benchmark you put in front of it, sometimes within months.

But there's a utility problem. These models beat world champions at Go, score highly on the SAT or bar exams, and solve olympiad-level math, yet the world's GDP hasn't changed that much. Why?

I think it's because the way we evaluate models is very different from how the real world works, in a few important ways.

First, our benchmarks usually assume tasks are **autonomous**. You give the model an input, it runs on its own, and you grade the output. In the real world, almost no valuable work happens that way. A software engineer or a customer service agent constantly interacts with people: clarifying what they want, getting feedback, adjusting. Humans are in the loop the whole time. If your evaluation removes the human, you're not measuring what actually matters for creating value.

Second, our benchmarks assume tasks are **i.i.d.** You have 500 test problems, you run them independently, and you average the score. But real work is sequential. A human gets better at a job over time because they accumulate context: they learn the codebase, the company, and the user's preferences. Today's models mostly start from zero every time. They're like a very smart new intern who shows up every morning with amnesia. Intelligence isn't the bottleneck there. Memory, context, and the ability to learn on the job are.

So in the "second half," I think the most important question shifts from "can we train a model to solve X?" to "what should we actually be training AI to do, and how do we measure real progress?" Evaluation becomes more important than training. We need to design tasks and environments that look more like real-world utility. They should involve real users and long horizons, and they should reward the model for getting better over time, not just for one-shot correctness.

There's also a product side. Value doesn't come only from the model. It comes from how the model fits into a workflow, what interface it has, what tools it can use, and who it's working for. In many cases the model is already capable enough, but the environment, the product, and the incentives haven't been built around it yet.

So my short answer is that we've become very good at solving exams, but the economy isn't an exam. To close that gap, we need to change the games we're playing, not just get better at playing the old ones.

r001.rationale: The response identifies limited memory and context as a bottleneck behind models’ limited economic impact, saying models start from zero while people accumulate workplace context.

r002.rationale: It discusses human interaction and accumulated context but does not say social context is distributed across people’s minds.

r003.rationale: It does not state that human social context cannot be fully captured in writing.

r004.rationale: It does not compare a person’s reasoning ability with o3 or say workplace context lets a weaker reasoner outperform it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we've been optimizing for the wrong thing, or at least a thing that was easy to measure rather than a thing that is actually valuable.

Look at what the models are good at: math olympiad problems, coding competitions, Go, standardized exams. What do all of these have in common? They're closed worlds. The problem is fully specified, the environment is clean, there's a clear reward signal, and critically, the task is short. You get the question, you think, you answer, done. We've gotten extremely good at that regime, and the benchmarks reflect it. But most economic value in the real world doesn't look like that at all.

Real work is long-horizon. A real task might take a person a week, and involve dozens of interactions with messy systems, emails, half-broken tools, people who change their minds. The information you need isn't handed to you; you have to go find it, and often you don't even know what you don't know. There's no ground truth at the end that says "correct." The feedback is delayed, noisy, sometimes it never comes at all. So a model that's a genius at a two-hour exam can still fall apart on something as mundane as "handle this customer's refund end to end," because the hard part isn't the reasoning, it's everything around the reasoning.

I'd put it this way: we solved the "thinking" problem before we solved the "acting" problem. Reasoning as a capability is largely there. What's missing is agency in the full sense: memory that persists across days, the ability to recover from your own mistakes mid-task, knowing when to ask versus when to just proceed, operating in environments that weren't designed for you. Those are not things you get for free from scaling pretraining or from RL on math. They require training in environments that actually look like the world, with the mess included.

And there's a second piece, which is less about the models and more about the ecosystem. Even where the capability exists, the interfaces, the trust, the evaluation methods, the organizational willingness to let a system actually do things instead of just suggest things, all of that lags. A lot of current deployment is "AI writes a draft, human checks it," which caps the value at roughly the cost of a human's time saved on a draft. The real value unlock is when you can delegate outcomes, not drafts, and we're not there yet because we can't yet reliably measure whether an agent did the job well.

So I'm actually fairly optimistic, because I don't think this is a fundamental limitation. I think it's a mismatch between what we've been measuring and what matters. The next phase is about building the right environments and the right evaluations, so that "good at the benchmark" and "good at the job" finally become the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response attributes limited economic value to short, clean benchmarks and gaps in long-horizon agency and deployment. It does not propose missing context as a fundamental reason, and it says the problem is not a fundamental limitation.

r002.rationale: It discusses messy systems and people changing their minds, but does not state that human social context is distributed across people's minds.

r003.rationale: It says needed information may have to be found, but does not claim that human social context cannot be fully captured in writing.

r004.rationale: It does not compare workplace performance with o3 or say that a person with weaker reasoning can outperform it through workplace context.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a gap between being able to solve a problem and being able to do a job. In an exam or a game, someone has already defined the objective, given you the relevant information, and specified how success will be measured. You can focus entirely on finding the answer.

In real work, those conditions usually don’t exist. You have to figure out what the problem is, gather information from different places, use tools, coordinate with people, and recognize when you’ve made a mistake. Reasoning is one part of that process. Even very strong reasoning doesn’t automatically give you the ability to complete the whole process reliably.

And economic value depends on the whole process. If a model produces something impressive but a person still has to check every step and fix the result, the actual savings can be small. A benchmark score can improve substantially without changing how much work someone can delegate.

So I think the next challenge is to turn intelligence into reliable action in real environments. We need to ask not just, ‘Can the model answer this question?’ but, ‘Can it take responsibility for a useful task from beginning to end, at a cost that makes sense?’ That’s where the connection to economic value becomes much more direct.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts exams, where objectives and relevant information are supplied, with real work, where people must identify problems and gather information. It presents that gap as a reason strong reasoning alone has not yielded economic value.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that human social context is distributed across people's minds.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that human social context cannot be fully captured in writing.

r004.rationale: The response does not compare a person with weaker reasoning ability to o3 or claim that such a person can outperform it at work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a gap between being able to solve a problem and being able to do a job. In an exam or a game, the objective is clear, the rules are fixed, and you get feedback on whether you succeeded. Most economically valuable work doesn’t look like that. You have to figure out what the problem is, gather context, use tools, coordinate with people, and check whether what you did actually helped.

Reasoning is an important part of that, but it’s only one part. A model might give an excellent answer when you put all the relevant information into its context. In a company, that information is scattered across documents, software systems, and people’s heads. Getting it and acting on it reliably can be harder than answering the question itself.

Reliability also matters differently. If an agent performs each step correctly most of the time, it can still fail frequently on a task with many steps. And if someone has to supervise everything and repair the mistakes, the productivity gain becomes much smaller.

So I think the bottleneck is turning intelligence into reliable action in real environments. We need to look beyond whether a model can answer a difficult question and ask whether it can complete useful work, end to end, at a cost that makes sense.

r001.rationale: The response identifies workplace information as scattered across documents, systems, and people’s heads, and says obtaining and acting on it can be harder than answering a question. It presents this as part of the bottleneck limiting economic value.

r002.rationale: It says relevant workplace information is scattered across systems and people’s heads, conveying that context is distributed across people’s minds.

r003.rationale: The response says information is scattered, but does not state that social context cannot be fully captured in writing.
